opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the most important thing is that I don't really think of it as "persuading." When I go into a room with an investor, I'm trying to figure out whether we see the same future. If we do, the conversation almost runs itself. If we don't, no amount of pitching is going to fix that, and it's better for both of us to find out early.

So I usually start with the big picture. What I believe is that mathematics is going to be one of the first domains where AI becomes truly superhuman, because math has something most fields don't: you can verify the answer. With formal languages like Lean, a proof either checks or it doesn't. There's no hallucination you can hide behind. That gives you a really clean reward signal, and it means you can build systems that reason, check themselves, and improve. Once investors understand that, they start to see why this isn't a niche academic project. It's a path toward reliable reasoning, and reliable reasoning matters for software verification, chip design, finance, science, and many other areas.

The second thing is the team. Early-stage investors are really betting on people. So I talk a lot about why we are the right group to do this. You need people who deeply understand mathematics, people who are excellent at AI research, and people who can build serious infrastructure. Those are usually different communities that don't talk to each other much. Being able to bring them together is a big part of our story.

The third thing is being honest about what's hard. I don't pretend there's no risk. Formal math data is scarce, the problems are genuinely difficult, and timelines in research are uncertain. I've found that the best investors actually respect that. They've heard a thousand pitches where everything is perfect. When you can clearly say, "Here's the hardest part, and here's how we're attacking it," it builds a lot more trust.

And finally, I try to be myself. I'm a math person at heart, so sometimes I get very excited and go deep into technical details. Some investors love that, and some people's eyes glaze over a little, which is fine. It helps me find the partners who are genuinely curious about the problem, and those are the people you want with you for the long journey.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they assess whether they and the investor see the same future, but does not clearly present the investor as persuading themselves to invest.

r002.rationale: The candidate frames the conversation around whether founder and investor share the same future and describes aligned investors as partners for the long journey.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try not to think of it as persuading. When I started raising for Axiom, I had this instinct that I needed to pitch, to sell, to convince people that AI for mathematics was going to be huge. And the first few conversations went badly because of that. I was performing, and the investors could feel it.

What changed is that I started treating fundraising as a filtering process rather than a conversion process. My job isn't to get everyone to say yes. My job is to find the small number of people who already believe something close to what I believe about the world, and then show them, as precisely as I can, what we're actually doing and why it's hard.

So in practice, I lead with the problem. I'll say: mathematics is the one domain where you can verify truth completely, where there's no ambiguity about whether an output is correct. If you can build a system that genuinely reasons there, you've built something that matters far beyond math. Some investors hear that and their eyes light up. Others nod politely and ask about revenue in year two. Both responses are useful data. I'm not going to spend my energy trying to drag the second group across the line, because even if I succeed, they'll be the wrong partners when things get difficult.

The second thing I've learned is to be very honest about what I don't know. I come from a research background, and in research you're trained to state your assumptions and your open questions. I bring that into the room. I'll say, here is the technical risk, here is what we haven't solved, here is what I'm uncertain about on the commercial side. Counterintuitively, that builds more trust than a polished narrative. Sophisticated investors have seen a thousand confident decks. What they haven't seen as often is a founder who can map the landscape of risk clearly and still wants to walk into it.

And then the last piece is the team and the people around us. Investors are ultimately making a bet on whether this specific group of humans can do something that hasn't been done. So I spend a lot of time talking about who we've brought together, what they've already accomplished, and why they chose to work on this rather than the dozen easier things they could be doing. That tends to say more than any slide I could make.

So if I had to compress it: don't persuade, filter. Be precise about the problem. Be honest about the risk. And let the people speak for themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising is a filtering process for investors who already share the founder’s beliefs, but it does not clearly say investors persuade themselves to invest.

r002.rationale: The response seeks aligned investors and describes their investment as a bet on the team, but it does not frame fundraising as an invitation to collaborate on a shared undertaking.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is understanding what the investor needs to believe. Do they have doubts about the problem, the timing, or whether this team can execute? Those are different conversations, and giving the same pitch to everyone won’t necessarily address them.

I’d focus on explaining the opportunity clearly: here’s the problem, here’s our insight, and here’s the evidence that gives us confidence. Then I’d be honest about what we still need to figure out. You want someone to understand both the ambition and the reasoning behind it.

And I’d treat it as a conversation. Asking what someone finds unconvincing can be much more useful than adding another five slides. Sometimes you can address the concern; sometimes it reveals that you’re looking for different things in a partnership.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding and addressing investors’ doubts, but does not clearly present investors as persuading themselves to invest.

r002.rationale: It mentions that differing expectations may reveal a poor partnership fit, but does not frame fundraising as an invitation to collaborate on a shared undertaking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of fundraising as finding alignment. You need to explain what you’re building, why it matters, and why you’re the right person to build it. But you also need to understand the investor—what they care about, what concerns they have, and what evidence would help them make a decision.

I try to be clear about both the ambition and the uncertainty. Here’s the opportunity we see, here’s what we’ve learned so far, and here’s what the next round of funding would allow us to prove. You want someone who understands the risks and still shares your conviction.

r001.rationale: The response says the founder should understand the investor and provide evidence to help them decide, but it does not present investors as persuading themselves to invest.

r002.rationale: The response describes fundraising as finding alignment and seeking an investor who shares the founder’s conviction, but it does not frame it as an invitation to collaborate on the same undertaking.
